title: Antibody-drug conjugates: unpacking toxicity profiles and optimized designs for enhanced safety and antitumor efficacy.
summary: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have expanded treatment options across multiple malignancies, but their clinical benefit remains constrained by heterogeneous and sometimes serious toxicities. These toxicities rarely arise from a single component; instead, they reflect the association between target biology, molecular architecture, systemic exposure, and tissue susceptibility. We first examine the structural basis of ADC toxicity by discussing the distinct contributions of the antibody-target axis, linker, payload, drug loading, and conjugation strategy to systemic exposure and tissue toxicity. We distinguish organ-selective "on-target, off-tumor" injury from target-independent toxicity and further characterize two major off-target routes: context-dependent uptake of intact ADCs through Fcγ receptor-mediated or pinocytosis-dominant pathways, and spatially distinct exposure to released payload arising from premature systemic release or localized bystander diffusion. Furthermore, we summarize a multidisciplinary management framework, ranging from prophylactic measures to graded interventions across complex scenarios such as treatment rechallenge and combination therapy. Finally, we discuss strategies to widen the therapeutic window through exposure-response-guided dosing, next-generation molecular engineering, and emerging conjugate platforms. Artificial intelligence and computational approaches may further extend safety optimization from drug design to patient stratification and real-world surveillance. By linking molecular design, spatial exposure, and clinical management, this review provides an integrated framework to improve ADC safety while preserving antitumor efficacy.

title: Artificial intelligence for vascular minimally invasive surgery: techniques, clinical integration, and challenges.
summary: Minimally invasive surgery (MIS), including endovascular and robot-assisted procedures, is widely used for vascular pathologies but remains limited by technical complexity, cognitive workload, and postoperative complications. Artificial Intelligence (AI) may help address these challenges through predictive analysis, decision support, image analysis, and automation. A structured Google Scholar search was conducted from February 21, 2025, to January 1, 2026, and updated through September 2026. Peer-reviewed studies applying AI to vascular MIS were included, with additional targeted searches addressing clinical translation, deployment, regulation, and ethical considerations. Thirty primary studies were analyzed, including eight on machine learning, nine on deep learning, four on natural language processing, and nine on robotics or reinforcement learning. Machine learning supported risk stratification and outcome prediction, deep learning enabled imaging and segmentation applications, natural language processing facilitated clinical information extraction, and robotic systems supported navigation and procedural assistance. AI demonstrates substantial potential across the vascular MIS pathway, but broader clinical adoption requires stronger validation, prospective multicenter studies, standardized reporting, health-economic evaluation, and careful consideration of regulatory, liability, and accessibility challenges.

title: Multimodal imaging and artificial intelligence for bone tumor diagnosis: Comparative performance and emerging technologies.
summary: Multimodal imaging is central to the diagnosis, staging, and management of bone tumors. Radiography and computed tomography remain essential for initial assessment and cortical evaluation, magnetic resonance imaging provides superior soft tissue contrast and local staging accuracy, and positron emission tomography enhances detection of metastatic disease and treatment response. No single technique suffices across clinical scenarios. Advances in artificial intelligence and radiomics offer avenues to augment this framework, with demonstrated potential in lesion classification, segmentation, prognostication, and response prediction. This review advances a specific argument rather than surveying available technologies: that the principal constraint on artificial intelligence in musculoskeletal oncology is the stability of the reference standard rather than algorithmic capability. Ground truth in bone tumors is unstable on four grounds. Core needle biopsy samples a limited volume and may miss the highest-grade component: agreement between biopsy and resection grade in central chondrosarcoma falls from a weighted kappa of 0.63 in long bones to 0.12 in the pelvis. Expert interpretation is itself inconsistent, with interobserver kappa for grading cartilaginous tumors of 0.44 among musculoskeletal pathologists and 0.35 among radiologists. Molecular criteria have redefined entities within the past decade, so older datasets contain classes that no longer exist as defined. And histological classification does not reliably predict clinical behavior. Consequently, measurable accuracy has a ceiling set by the reference standard rather than the algorithm, and apparent failure on external validation may reflect label divergence between institutions rather than model deficiency. Evidence is graded throughout, and clinical readiness distinguished from technical performance. No system for primary bone tumor characterization has regulatory clearance in the United States or Europe, and formal appraisal of this literature confirms low methodological compliance and infrequent external validation. Progress will depend on multicenter validation and protocol harmonization, and, distinctively for this field, on composite reference standards, outcome-based endpoints, and explicit uncertainty modelling, since ground-truth instability can be mitigated but not eliminated.

title: Navigating the promise and peril: Concerns, limitations, and risks of artificial intelligence in medicine.
Vibrational spectroscopy and artificial intelligence for dynamic phenotypic characterization of antimicrobial resistance.
summary: The rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance has created an urgent need for diagnostic technologies capable of rapidly identifying resistant phenotypes and informing precision antimicrobial therapy. Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing methods remain clinically reliable; however, they are limited by relatively long turnaround times and restricted physiological resolution. In recent years, vibrational spectroscopy techniques have emerged as promising platforms for rapid phenotypic microbiology because they generate label-free biochemical fingerprints associated with proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and membrane biomolecules. When integrated with machine learning and artificial intelligence, these technologies could provide highly sensitive tools for rapid bacterial classification, resistance prediction, and monitoring of dynamic physiological adaptation during antibiotic exposure. This review discusses the integration of chemometrics, machine learning, and deep learning algorithms with spectroscopic datasets, emphasizing both predictive performance and biological interpretability. It is highly useful for bacterial identification, biochemical characterization, and resistance profiling across multiple microbial species. Major controversies regarding genotype-versus-phenotype diagnostics, reproducibility, standardization, and AI explainability are also examined. Finally, we highlight current research gaps and future directions, including single-cell spectroscopy, multimodal phenotyping, explainable AI frameworks, and approaches in systems microbiology. Taken together, the available evidence indicates that integrating vibrational spectroscopy with artificial intelligence could substantially reshape future antimicrobial resistance diagnostics and mechanistic microbiology.

title: Patient engagement, acceptability, and preference of artificial intelligence versus human coaching for diabetes prevention.
summary: Artificial intelligence-powered lifestyle interventions may expand access to behavioral change support, but patient experience remains critical to real-world uptake and effectiveness. In a phase 3 randomized clinical trial of adults with prediabetes and overweight or obesity (N = 368), we compared a fully automated AI-driven diabetes prevention program (DPP) with a CDC-recognized human-coach-based DPP. Participants assigned to the AI-led DPP initiated the intervention sooner (median 11 vs 26 days; p < 0.001) and demonstrated higher and more evenly distributed engagement over 12 months. Acceptability ratings were consistently higher for the human-led DPP across all domains, with the largest differences in satisfaction (p < 0.001). Preference responses also favored human coaching, with 46.5% of AI-assigned participants indicating they would have preferred a human coach compared with 31.5% preferring a fully automated program in the human-led group (p = 0.012). These findings illustrate a trade-off between scalability and perceived quality of experience. Clinical trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05056376 (registered September 24, 2021).

title: Artificial intelligence in digital pathology: Principles, applications, challenges, and future directions.
summary: This article provides an overview of digital pathology and its evolving role in modern diagnostic practice. We begin by comparing conventional microscopy with digital pathology and outlining the major components of the digital pathology workflow. We then explore whole-slide imaging, its imaging modalities, scanner technologies, image storage, and image management systems. We then examine the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital pathology, discussing current AI applications and the spectrum of computational approaches, from conventional feature-engineering methods to deep learning and multimodal models. Finally, we review the clinical applications of digital pathology, summarize its implementation across US medical centers, and discuss the technical, regulatory, and operational challenges that must be addressed for broader clinical adoption.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Gallbladder Carcinoma: A Review of Research Studies and Clinical Evidence.
summary: Gallbladder carcinoma (GBC) is the most common biliary tract malignancy and is usually diagnosed at an advanced stage. Artificial intelligence (AI), including radiomics, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), is increasingly applied to its diagnosis, surgical management and prognostication, but how far the reported performance can be trusted is unclear. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and Google Scholar were searched to 5 May 2026 using database-specific search strategies. Each primary prediction-model study was characterized separately by design, number of centers and validation type (internal, temporal or external). Of 31 primary AI studies in GBC, 29 were retrospective, 22 were single-center and 24 reported internal validation only. In independent test or external cohorts, DL and ML models discriminated benign from malignant gallbladder lesions with areas under the curve (AUCs) of approximately 0.80-0.89; a multicenter model distinguishing xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis from GBC achieved an external AUC of 0.88, and automated computed tomography (CT) segmentation an external Dice score of 0.76. The best recurrence model achieved an AUC of 0.76 on internal (random-split) validation; none of the reviewed prognostic models reported a quantified external-validation estimate. Intraoperative AI is technically feasible but has no outcome data, and federated learning has been tested only in simulation. AI could plausibly assist several steps of GBC care, but the evidence is dominated by retrospective, single-center, internally validated studies from Asia, and metrics from different studies are not directly comparable. Prospective multicenter external validation, shared annotated datasets and standardized reporting are required before clinical adoption.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Diagnosis, Endotyping and Risk Stratification in Obstructive Sleep Apnea.
summary: Multimodal data inputs available in sleep-related investigations positions sleep medicine as an ideal discipline for the impactful use of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Using AI to help diagnose OSA can reduce wait times and lead to earlier diagnosis and treatment. Big data can allow for detailed analysis of patient characteristics using AI and can aid in sub-categorizing patients. AI is an important tool that could be used to augment sleep providers to: improve workflow, bridge the gap between symptom onset and diagnosis, and facilitate a precision care approach to our patients.

title: Can AI Help Repurpose Drugs to Fight Against Antibiotic Resistance?
summary: Drug repurposing and development to meet the threat of antimicrobial resistance can be costly and time-consuming, but AI models may be able to help. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Sara Novak reports on recent research training models to identify candidate drugs to treat resistant infections.

title: Factors influencing registered nurses' attitudes toward and literacy in artificial intelligence: a cross-sectional systematic review.
summary: Presently, artificial intelligence technology is being extensively applied across clinical nursing practice. However, whether this technology can be deeply integrated into clinical workflows depends largely on nurses' attitudes and literacy regarding artificial intelligence. Consequently, conducting an in depth exploration of core factors shaping registered nurses' artificial intelligence attitudes and literacy holds significant importance for driving the rapid development of intelligent nursing. This study strictly adhered to PRISMA guidelines. Systematic searches were conducted across seven English databases, namely PubMed, Web of Science, Medline, Embase, The Cochrane Library, IEEE Xplore, and CINAHL, alongside three Chinese databases, including China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), Wanfang Data, and VIP Database. The search timeframe ranged from database inception through May 30, 2026. Following screening according to inclusion and exclusion criteria, independent factors influencing attitudes and literacy were extracted. Employing a narrative synthesis approach, these influencing factors were categorized, summarized, and narratively integrated across distinct thematic domains. A total of 30 studies involving 12,958 registered nurses were included in this systematic review. The majority of the studies were conducted in China and Turkey. The independent factors influencing registered nurses' attitudes toward artificial intelligence included educational attainment, age, length of service, gender, professional title/nursing level, hospital tier/category, AI awareness/understanding/knowledge, AI training experience, AI usage experience, artificial intelligence anxiety, and digital leadership. The factors independently affecting nurses' artificial intelligence literacy included leadership style, AI training experience, and usage experience/frequency. Current evidence indicates that key modifiable factors to improve nurses' attitudes toward and literacy in artificial intelligence include AI-related training, practical hands-on experience, and organizational leadership, while technical anxiety should not be overlooked. Compared with demographic characteristics, educational and experiential interventions appear more effective in enhancing nurses' artificial intelligence literacy levels. Nursing managers should actively implement smart training programs, increase opportunities for nurses to apply new technologies in clinical practice, and formulate relevant policies regarding data privacy protection and accountability division, thereby promoting the safe and effective integration of AI technology into patient care. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/recorddashboard.

title: Patient-reported outcomes, predictive modeling, and artificial intelligence in spine surgery: current limitations and future directions.
summary: Chronic back pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide, contributing to reduced productivity and diminished quality of life for many patients. Spine surgery, particularly lumbar decompression and fusion, serves as an intensive intervention after conservative measures fail. Despite advances in surgical technique and instrumentation, outcomes remain highly variable, with up to half of patients experiencing little or no meaningful improvement. This variability has prompted growing interest in predictive models that forecast which patients are most likely to benefit from surgery. This review examines the current landscape of predictive modeling for patient-reported outcomes (PROs) in spine surgery. We evaluated the use of PRO instruments, which have become central to assessing surgical success. We further explored existing predictive models that incorporate demographic, clinical, and psychosocial variables, as well as emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning techniques aimed at improving diagnostic accuracy and prognostic performance. Current predictive models demonstrate variable performance across populations and remain constrained by incomplete datasets, inconsistencies in definitions, and limited integration of psychosocial factors. While most models report moderate discrimination for categorical outcomes (AUC 0.62-0.84), the subjective nature of PROs and the complexity of postoperative recovery pose challenges to accurate prediction. Machine-learning approaches, including neural networks, show promise in identifying complex relationships among diverse predictors of surgical outcomes. Future advancements will rely on leveraging multimodal data sources and integrating them through AI-driven frameworks. Transparency and external validation remain essential for clinical implementation. While PROs remain essential for understanding patient experiences and benchmarking surgical success, they often fall short as standalone predictive tools. The next generation of modeling should integrate multidimensional data and utilize AI's capacity to detect clinically meaningful patterns. When implemented, these models have the potential to enhance preoperative counseling, guide surgical decision-making, and advance personalized spine care.

title: Machine Learning in Smart Hydrogel 4D Printing: Advances, Challenges, and Translational Perspectives.
summary: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and smart hydrogel-based additive manufacturing offers new capabilities for fabricating adaptive structures, though the field remains in early stages of translation. Smart hydrogels, with their stimuli-responsive properties and biocompatibility, present opportunities in tissue engineering, drug delivery, and soft robotics. However, the complexity of their material behavior and the challenges of high-resolution four-dimensional (4D) printing demand advanced computational approaches to optimize design, processing, and performance. This review systematically examines the role of AI, encompassing machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and generative models, in addressing these challenges. We critically assess AI-driven strategies for hydrogel formulation, real-time process control, structural optimization, and biological outcome prediction, distinguishing between retrospectively fitted models and prospectively validated implementations. A key contribution of this review is the clear differentiation between AI-assisted 3D printing and genuine 4D printing, where constructs exhibit time-dependent shape change, actuation, or degradation in response to stimuli. We introduce AI applications in specific hydrogel printing domains, provide a comparative framework for distinguishing 3D from 4D systems, and critically evaluate quantitative claims with attention to dataset size, validation approaches, and reproducibility. Case studies highlight where AI enhances printability, resolution, and functional outcomes, while we also identify persistent limitations including data scarcity, model interpretability, and regulatory hurdles. A comparative analysis of AI-assisted versus traditional design-of-experiment strategies reveals that while AI offers advantages in high-dimensional spaces, traditional methods remain more accessible, interpretable, and reproducible for simpler systems. By synthesizing recent advancements with transparent methodology and practical guidance, this study provides a roadmap for future research at the intersection of AI and smart hydrogel additive manufacturing, advocating for interdisciplinary collaboration and standardized reporting to enable next-generation innovations.

title: Machine learning for RNA-small molecule interactions: methodologies, evaluation, and future directions.
summary: RNA is emerging as a compelling therapeutic target due to its rich structural diversity and central involvement in gene regulation, splicing, translation, and cellular signaling. Alongside advances in structural biology, computational approaches, especially machine learning and deep learning, have transformed the systematic analysis of RNA-small molecule interactions. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive survey of computational methods for RNA-small molecule interaction prediction, with a particular emphasis on three core tasks: binding site prediction, binding preference prediction, and binding pose prediction. We first summarize the data resources commonly used to support these tasks and outline molecular representations that capture RNA structural features and the chemical properties of small molecules. We then review a spectrum of computational approaches for the above three tasks, ranging from statistical methods and traditional machine learning to deep learning. We further evaluate representative methods for each task, providing insights into their respective strengths and limitations. Finally, we highlight open challenges in current research on RNA-small molecule interactions, including limited data availability, the black-box nature of the models, and the growing need for generative modeling. We discuss emerging directions such as data augmentation, model interpretability, and RNA-targeted small-molecule design as promising pathways to address these challenges and advance rational RNA-targeted drug discovery.

title: Clinical predictions using artificial intelligence in neurosurgery and its subspecialties: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) models for clinical prediction are proliferating across neurosurgery, but their aggregate discriminative performance, distribution along the care pathway and methodological quality are unclear. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed these studies in neurosurgery and its subspecialities along with their risk of bias appraisal. We performed a PRISMA search on PubMed and Ovid for peer-reviewed original studies (2015-2026) using AI to predict a clinical outcome in neurosurgical populations. Metrics (primary- AUC; secondary- accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, c-index) were pooled using random effects modelling, overall, by subspeciality and care-pathway stage. Each study was classified as diagnostic, prognostic or forecasting and was assigned an evidence level. Clinical prediction task sub-stratification analysis was performed. Risk-of-bias was assessed using PROBAST. PROSPERO registered: CRD420261436614. 1063 studies were included. Across 451 (42.2%) studies reporting AUC, pooled discrimination was 0.86 (95% CI: 0.849-0.862), ranging from 0.84 (spine) to 0.87 (neuro-oncology), with extreme heterogeneity (I2 98.6%, τ2=0.27; 95% prediction interval: 0.68-0.94). Performance varied by clinical pathway stage, highest for diagnosis, grading and molecular tasks and lowest for post-operative tasks; pre-diagnosis, pre-operative and intra-operative applications were sparse, and treatment models were confined to neuro-oncology. Only 51 studies (4.8%) were using prospective data with external validation, whereas 619 (58%) rested on internal validation alone or no validation. 89% studies were at high risk-of-bias, driven by the analysis domain. Pooled discrimination was unchanged (AUC: 0.86%) when restricted to externally validated or non-high-risk studies. AI models report high performance across all the neurosurgical subspecialities, concordant across AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity and robust to risk-of-bias stratification. Performance is highest for imaging-anchored diagnostic tasks and lowest at decision-facing post-operative stage. However, the literature is dominated by optimism-prone, internally-validated and poorly calibrated models with extreme heterogeneity. External validation, calibration analysis and reporting guidelines adherence remain prerequisites for clinical adoption.

title: Artificial intelligence-generated and algorithmically personalized music interventions and their effects on brain function, behavior, and health: a critical review.
summary: This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener's own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Neurology: A Critical Narrative Review of Clinical Evidence, Translation, and Responsible Implementation.
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to neuroimaging, electrophysiology, clinical text, and digitally measured behavior, but reported performance often exceeds the maturity of clinical evidence. We conducted a structured narrative review, informed by SANRA principles, of English-language human studies, reviews, and regulatory sources identified in PubMed/MEDLINE and IEEE Xplore from January 2022 through July 2026; older landmark studies were retained when necessary for historical or methodological context. We applied a common translational-evidence framework across six prespecified neurological domains to distinguish technical performance from external validation, prospective clinical evaluation, implementation, and demonstrated patient benefit. Evidence was appraised according to cohort representativeness, patient-level data separation, external and prospective validation, calibration, clinical comparators, regulatory status, workflow integration, and patient-level benefit. Across stroke, dementia, Parkinson disease, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, and neuro-oncology, the strongest evidence concerns narrowly defined imaging and signal-processing tasks. A cluster-randomized stroke study demonstrated shorter thrombectomy workflow time, and several externally validated models show improved portability. In contrast, many high-accuracy classification and segmentation studies remain retrospective, single-dataset, internally validated, and uncalibrated. Multimodal learning, foundation models, federated learning, and large language models broaden capability but introduce additional risks related to dataset shift, bias, opacity, privacy, and automation. Neuro-AI should be judged by its intended clinical task and evidence maturity rather than headline accuracy. Multicenter external validation, prospective workflow evaluation, calibration, subgroup reporting, human-factors testing, and post-deployment surveillance are prerequisites for safe and equitable clinical use.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pre-anaesthetic Evaluation and Perioperative Planning: A Narrative Review.
summary: Preanesthetic evaluation is essential for perioperative safety, yet it remains time-consuming, heavily reliant on documentation, and vulnerable to variability in data collection, risk assessment, and clinical decision-making. The increase in surgical cases, patient complexity, and digital health records has created opportunities for artificial intelligence (AI) to assist anesthesiologists in preoperative screening, risk assessment, and perioperative planning. New AI applications in anesthesiology include machine learning models for predicting perioperative risks, natural language processing (NLP) systems for extracting key information from unstructured records, and large language model (LLM)-based tools for documentation support and structured clinical summaries. Studies indicate these systems may enhance workflow efficiency, expand preanesthetic data collection, aid ASA physical status classification, and generate structured recommendations for investigations, optimization, and anesthetic plans, all with clinician oversight. This review explores the current role of AI in preanesthetic evaluation and perioperative planning, focusing on practical uses such as automated history synthesis, investigation choices, risk stratification, preoperative orders, and personalized anesthetic decision support. It also addresses system limitations like hallucination, bias, privacy issues, lack of explainability, and medicolegal concerns. Based on current evidence, AI is best suited as a decision-support tool for clinicians rather than a standalone replacement for anesthesiologists.

title: Deep learning-based CT lesion analysis and radiological burden stratification in clinically diagnosed ventilator-associated pneumonia.
summary: Ventilator associated pneumonia (VAP) is a major complication in the intensive care unit (ICU) and requires objective computed tomography (CT) evaluation. Therefore, this article conducted a retrospective research analysis and developed a multimodal deep learning framework. Firstly, this retrospective study included 512 patients clinically diagnosed with VAP, and then utilized a developed multimodal deep learning framework for voxel-level lesion segmentation, multi-label radiological discovery classification, and radiological burden grading. This framework integrates the anatomical priors of TotalSegmenter, a three-dimensional (3D) Swin UNETR multitasking network, and cross attention fusion of CT features and ventilation parameters. Ultimately, the study showed that the Dice score for internal validation was 0.847, the macroscopic mean area (AUC) under the subject's working characteristic curve was 0.919, and the weighted kappa was 0.826. External validation showed a Dice score of 0.821, with no significant difference between scanner manufacturers. After adjusting for clinical covariates, including acute physiology and chronic health assessment II (APACHE II) scores, there was still a significant correlation between radiation load level and 28 day mortality (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.34, P < 0.001), supporting its potential prognostic relevance.

title: Automation and artificial intelligence in the clinical microbiology laboratory.
summary: Clinical microbiology laboratories face persistent pressure to shorten turnaround times, reduce manual workloads, and standardize diagnostic workflows. Total laboratory automation (TLA) and artificial intelligence (AI) are complementary responses to these demands. In this review, we examine how the evidence base for automation and AI in clinical microbiology is distributed along a maturity gradient and what this distribution implies for the next phase of implementation. Available evidence indicates that automated platforms shorten culture turnaround times and reduce manual workload in observational and multi-center studies, although the scale of benefit depends on specimen type and workflow configuration. Automated reading, identification, and susceptibility testing systems showed high concordance with manual standards for common specimen types, with error rates below commonly cited acceptability thresholds. Evidence for AI performance in plate reading and resistance prediction is abundant; however, most models remain in an assistive phase without prospective validation. Randomized trials of rapid testing and automation rarely demonstrate overall clinical superiority, and patient-oriented benefits remain limited and inconsistent. Guidelines provide directional support, whereas interoperability, quality control, and regulatory frameworks are still under development. The priority of the field is not additional single-center performance validation. The next phase requires multi-center prospective verification, interpretability, standardization, and comparative evidence with clinical outcomes as endpoints. AI-assisted evidence tools may accelerate evidence generation, although their utility remains preliminary.

title: Deep Learning for AD Risk Screening and Progression Prediction.
summary: The rise of Alzheimer's disease (AD) immunotherapies underscores the need for accessible, time-efficient biomarkers for early diagnosis. MRI-based deep learning shows promise in this regard, yet few models have undergone comprehensive clinical validation. Using the SILCODE cohort (722 Chinese participants, 1,105 scans), we test the transportability of our classifier (pretrained on Western samples) to an independent Chinese cohort without retraining. The associations between risk scores and disease progression, cognitive performance, and plasma biomarkers are examined. In addition, an interpretable framework is developed to generate individualized brain risk maps and identify subtypes. The model classifies AD with an AUC of 0.913 and 95.2% sensitivity, identifying 90.5% of high-risk individuals 2-3 years before clinical diagnosis. Risk scores correlate significantly with cognitive and plasma indices, particularly p-tau 217. Brain risk maps reveal AD subtypes, including a subgroup with rapid cognitive decline. These findings establish a population-robust, clinically relevant MRI-based model for early AD detection and risk stratification.

title: Machine learning in keratoconus: severity grading, progression prediction, and surgery outcomes.
summary: To review and evaluate machine learning (ML) applications in keratoconus (KC), with a focus on severity classification, progression prediction, and surgical outcome prediction. A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar for English-language studies published between January 2015 and October 2025. Studies applying ML to KC grading, progression prediction, or surgical outcome prediction were included. Data on clinical tasks, imaging modalities, model architectures, validation strategies, and performance were extracted and evaluated. Forty-one reports were identified, including 20 on severity classification, 10 on progression assessment, and 11 on surgical outcome prediction. Severity models mainly reproduced clinical or device-derived grades, while progression models addressed different endpoints, including tomographic change and subsequent corneal cross-linking. Surgical outcome models predicted optical changes, treatment response or graft outcomes at different follow-up intervals. ML showed promising internal performance for KC severity classification, while evidence for progression and surgical outcome prediction remains limited. Clinical translation will require standardized endpoints, patient-separated evaluation, multicenter external validation, calibration assessment, and direct comparison with existing clinical decision rules.

title: Updates in cardiovascular CT imaging in 2025: A year in review.
summary: The year 2025 brought long-term outcome data supporting coronary CT angiography (CCTA)-guided management of stable chest pain, a proposed reframing of coronary artery disease around atherosclerosis rather than ischemia, and the first large-scale real-world evaluation of a national artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled CT-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) program. This review summarizes selected advances in cardiovascular computed tomography (CCT) published in print or online during 2025. The studies span coronary artery disease outcomes and prevention, quantitative plaque analysis, photon-counting detector CT, coronary artery calcium scoring, pericoronary inflammation imaging, AI and machine learning, structural and congenital heart disease, and consensus and training documents. For each study we summarize the design, principal findings, limitations, and likely clinical implications, and we close with the barriers, including technical standardization, vendor-specific thresholds, equitable access, and the need for randomized outcome trials, that must be addressed before many of these advances can be implemented broadly.

title: Lectin Microarray-based Glycomics and Machine Learning Identify Shared Osteoarthritis Biomarkers in Humans, Dogs, and Horses.
summary: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis is a common sequela of joint injury in humans and companion animals, yet glycosylation changes associated with osteoarthritis remain poorly characterized. Lectin microarray analysis enables high-throughput profiling of glycan features in complex biofluids such as synovial fluid. Here, we used lectin microarrays to characterize synovial fluid glycosylation patterns in healthy and osteoarthritis-affected joints from horses, dogs, and humans. Comparative lectin-binding profiles within and across species revealed both conserved and species-specific glycomic signatures associated with osteoarthritis. Supervised machine learning distinguished osteoarthritis from control joints within a pooled multi-species framework and identified the lectins and their glycan epitopes contributing most strongly to classification, though cross-species generalization was limited and depended on the composition of each species' control cohort. Elevated high-mannose emerged as the shared glycomic signature across species. Together, these findings support the feasibility of synovial fluid glycomics, integrated with machine learning, for identifying conserved osteoarthritis-associated glycan signatures; and inform the design of glycan-based diagnostic and translational strategies in both veterinary and human medicine.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Sleep Medicine: From Bench Code to Bedside Care.
Artificial intelligence in healthcare: clinical applications, evidence maturity, risks, and life-cycle governance.
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used across clinical, administrative, and public health settings, but technical performance alone does not establish clinical utility, safety, equity, or sustainability. To critically analyze contemporary healthcare AI applications, characterize source types and non-ordinal evidence profiles in the supporting literature, synthesize key opportunities and risks, and identify governance requirements for clinically useful, safe, equitable, and responsible implementation. We conducted a critical narrative synthesis using PubMed, the Virtual Health Library, Web of Science, and Scopus as source-discovery tools on July 16, 2026. A curated corpus of 28 bibliographically verifiable publications was assembled judgmentally to provide complementary coverage of clinical applications, evidence characteristics, implementation, risk, and life-cycle governance. Sources were classified by primary design and non-mutually exclusive evidentiary domains, and the evidence described within them was characterized using non-ordinal profile categories. Findings were synthesized qualitatively because of substantial heterogeneity across technologies, settings, and source designs. The curated corpus addressed diagnosis and imaging, prediction and monitoring, clinical documentation, conversational systems, public health, hospital operations, and specialty applications. Within this assembled corpus, technical-performance/validation and process-utility/workflow domains were represented more often than clinical or patient-safety outcomes, economic outcomes, or post-deployment surveillance; these document-level counts are descriptive and have no inferential weight beyond the selected sources. Reported or proposed benefits included diagnostic support, personalization, documentation, surveillance, and workflow efficiency. Recurrent risks included poor generalizability, bias, miscalibration, hallucinations, opacity, privacy concerns, interoperability problems, inappropriate automation, unclear accountability, and hidden costs. Within this non-exhaustive corpus, the evidence more consistently supported assistive, context-specific uses than generalized autonomous replacement. Responsible implementation requires a clearly defined intended use, governed data, contextual validation, risk-proportionate human oversight, traceability, equity and safety assessment, continuous monitoring, and procedures to restrict, suspend, or withdraw systems when performance or implementation conditions change.

title: Digital and artificial intelligence-assisted medication management for older adults with chronic diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis aims to synthesize the results of randomized controlled trials to determine whether medication management approaches based on digital technologies and artificial intelligence/machine learning can indeed bring measurable clinical improvements in older adults with at least one chronic diseases. To identify relevant RCTs, we performed a systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, and other databases from their inception through June 30, 2026, for studies of digital and AI/ML-based medication management in older adults with at least one chronic diseases. All stages of study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers, applying the Cochrane RoB 2.0 tool. Meta-analytic pooling was conducted via RevMan 5.4. Nineteen RCTs met the inclusion criteria, of which 6 were included in the meta-analysis and 13 in the descriptive synthesis. For medication adherence, three studies reported highly heterogeneous results (I 2 = 97%), and because of this heterogeneity and the small number of studies, the data were not pooled; the individual study estimates ranged from SMD = -0.28-SMD = 1.89. For PIMs, only one study reported a comparable outcome; no pooled estimate was calculated. For hospitalization and mortality, the two included studies used different effect measures (HR and OR) and were therefore presented separately: Blum et al. reported an HR of 0.95 (95% CI 0.77-1.17), and Rieckert et al. reported an OR of 0.88 (95% CI 0.73-1.07). The current body of evidence does not establish clinically meaningful benefits of digital or AI/ML-based medication management on hard endpoints such as hospitalization and mortality among older adults with at least one chronic diseases. For medication adherence, the evidence remains inconclusive and highly heterogeneous, and no reliable pooled estimate could be obtained. Given the pronounced heterogeneity and the limited pool of high-quality RCTs, current evidence is insufficient to establish clinical benefit for the routine implementation of digital or AI/ML-based medication management systems in geriatric care and further rigorously designed studies are warranted. title: Artificial intelligence in Saudi otolaryngology research: a scoping review of the current landscape, gaps, and future directions.
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in otolaryngology, but the extent and focus of AI research in Saudi Arabia remain unclear. This scoping review mapped the available evidence and identified key research themes and knowledge gaps. A scoping review was conducted following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Saudi Medical Journal archive were searched for studies published between January 2019 and April 2026. Eligible studies investigated AI applications or clinician perspectives within Saudi otolaryngology. The evidence was mapped across major otolaryngology domains, including cochlear implantation and hearing, rhinology and skull base surgery, facial plastic surgery, laryngology and voice, head and neck oncology, surgical and other ENT-related interventions for obstructive sleep apnoea, AI education and implementation, and AI-assisted patient education. The searches identified 2,925 database records, four records from other sources and seven records from an updated search and expert suggestions; thirteen studies met the inclusion criteria. The evidence covered AI awareness and education, large language model (LLM)-based patient education, cochlear implantation, rhinology and skull base surgery, facial plastic surgery, laryngology and voice, and head and neck oncology; no eligible study addressed surgical or other ENT-related interventions for obstructive sleep apnoea. Clinicians were generally positive about AI, while clinical studies showed promising performance of AI models. LLM chatbots generally gave accurate postoperative advice, although, when validated tools were used, their responses were harder to read and less actionable than patient-education standards recommend. However, limited AI education, small or non-Saudi datasets, limited external validation, and implementation barriers remained important challenges. AI research in Saudi otolaryngology remains limited but is expanding across several clinical domains. Future research should prioritise Saudi-specific datasets, multicentre clinical validation, structured AI education, rigorous bilingual (Arabic and English) evaluation of LLM-generated patient information, and safe integration of AI into clinical practice in line with Saudi Vision 2030.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Arthroplasty: From Workflow Efficiency to Clinical Decision Support.
Patient-adaptive and clinically interpretable arrhythmia detection from ECG using lightweight hybrid deep learning.
summary: A precise and reliable identification of cardiac arrhythmias from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is critical for making informed clinical decisions. In this paper, a patient-adaptive and clinically interpretable a hybrid CNN-LSTM model with an attention mechanism is offered as a framework for ECG arrhythmia identification. The proposed framework combines signal preprocessing techniques with domain knowledge-driven morphological and time-frequency features to jointly analyze the waveform patterns and temporal dependencies in noisy ECG signals. In addition to beat-level classification, a composite arrhythmia burden score is also proposed to offer a patient-level summary of arrhythmic activity, and a lightweight patient-specific adaptation method is used to enhance reliability with limited calibration data. Over 99% accuracy and strong sensitivity to ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias are demonstrated by experimental results employing a rigorous inter-patient methodology on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. The suggested framework's capacity to generalize on actual clinical datasets is further validated by external validation on the PTB-XL dataset without retraining. The proposed framework is also scalable for cloud-based deployment to enable continuous ECG monitoring, thus emphasizing its potential for practical and patient-centric cardiac care.

title: Diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence in detecting periapical lesions: A comparative study with cone-beam computed tomography and conventional periapical radiography.
summary: Periapical lesions, particularly in their early stages, can be challenging to identify clinically and radiographically, as they may be asymptomatic or obscured by anatomical structures on conventional two-dimensional periapical radiography (2D PR). The diagnosis of periapical pathology may also be subjective and influenced by the examiner's experience, image quality, and interpretation variability. With recent technological advancements, artificial intelligence (AI)-based diagnostic tools have been introduced to support radiographic interpretation and improve the consistency of lesion detection. This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of AI in detecting periapical lesions by comparing its performance with 2D PR and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), using CBCT as the reference standard. This diagnostic accuracy study included 177 teeth from adult patients indicated for endodontic treatment. All teeth were examined using conventional 2D PR, CBCT, and AI-based image interpretation. The presence or absence of periapical pathology was recorded for each modality, and CBCT was considered the reference standard. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, overall accuracy, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis, and agreement testing. Compared with CBCT, AI showed a sensitivity of 84.16%, specificity of 93.42%, and accuracy of 88.14%. Conventional 2D PR showed lower sensitivity (64.36%) despite high specificity (100%). When periapical radiography was used as reference, AI demonstrated higher sensitivity (89.23%) but lower specificity (71.43%). CBCT remained the most reliable reference modality for detecting periapical lesions. AI demonstrated promising diagnostic accuracy and may support radiographic interpretation in endodontic practice.

title: A Systematic Review of Bias, Validation, and Explainability in Artificial Intelligence Algorithms for Dental Diagnostics.
summary: To critically evaluate the current role of artificial intelligence (AI) in dental diagnosis across multiple dental disciplines, assessing diagnostic performance, methodological quality, risk of bias, validation, explainability, and clinical applicability. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD42025639340). PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched up to December-2025. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment. Risk of bias in diagnostic accuracy studies was assessed using QUADAS-2-tool, evaluating the domains of patient selection, index test, reference standard, flow and timing whilst randomised studies were assessed using Cochrane RoB 2-tool. Reporting quality and transparency of AI-model development and validation were assessed using the selected items from TRIPOD-AI reporting guideline. Methodological quality and risk of bias in AI model development and evaluation were additionally assessed using PROBAST+AI. Ninety-six studies met the inclusion criteria, of which 90.6% were retrospective. Convolutional neural networks (CNN) were the most frequently used architecture (82.3%). Sixteen studies failed to specify the CNN architecture used. Reported diagnostic accuracy ranged from 81% to 99% across dental specialties, with high performance in implantology (92-99%), orthodontics (88-99%), endodontics (87-99%). Panoramic radiographs and cone-beam computed tomography were the most used imaging modalities. QUADAS-2 analysis indicated that high-risk of bias in 55.2% of studies and most lacked external validation, whilst Assessment using selected TRIPOD+AI items identified important gaps in reporting completeness and transparency, particularly in sample-size justification, missing-data handling, protocol availability, study registration, and data or code availability. AI demonstrates substantial technical capability to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. However, the predominance of retrospective designs, limited external validation, and methodological weaknesses constrain the strength of current evidence. The use of AI is potentially considered as a decision-support tool rather than replacement for clinical judgement.

title: Monotonic additive modeling reveals candidate biomarkers of cardio-renal-metabolic disorder susceptibility.
summary: Cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes mellitus form an interconnected disease continuum driven by shared risk factors, overlapping molecular pathways and reciprocal progression. This convergence has led to the recognition of cardio-renal-metabolic disorder (CRMD) as a unified systemic condition in which dysregulation of metabolic, vascular, inflammatory and renal pathways precedes organ-specific pathology. Despite this understanding, current diagnostic strategies remain disease-centric and are typically initiated after substantial tissue damage, limiting opportunities for early intervention. Identification of early non-invasive biomarkers capturing shared CRMD susceptibility is therefore of utmost clinical importance. In this study, we developed an explainable monotonic additive machine learning framework to identify blood-based molecular biomarkers associated with CRMD susceptibility. Transcriptomic profiles representing cardiovascular, renal and metabolic disease states were analysed within a unified CRMD paradigm. Following transcriptomic harmonization and batch correction, a monotonic additive XGBoost model combined with integrated biomarker score, gene-response analysis and differential expression analysis was implemented to identify biologically interpretable and directionally consistent biomarkers reflective of shared CRMD-associated dysregulation. Six biomarkers, including EEF1D, RPL27A, ERO1LB, JUN, POSTN and SERPINE2, were identified as potential CRMD susceptibility biomarkers spanning translational regulation, proteostasis, endoplasmic-reticulum function, systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, vascular dysfunction, extracellular remodeling and fibrosis. Importantly, these biomarkers have potential for blood-based detection using established assays such as ELISA, multiplex immunoassays and quantitative PCR, underscoring their translational potential for early CRMD screening, susceptibility assessment and risk stratification.

title: Demonstrating the accuracy and efficiency of artificial intelligence integrated workflows for primary breast cancer diagnosis: A comparative paired reader analysis.
summary: Evidence on the real-world impact of artificial intelligence (AI) decision support on diagnostic efficiency and workflow outcomes in primary breast cancer pathology remains limited. This retrospective, single-site, paired reader, two-arm study evaluated the impact of AI-assisted digital pathology (DP + AI) versus standard DP on workflow efficiency and diagnostic performance in digitized consecutive breast biopsy cases. Primary endpoints were pathologist review time, lab turnaround time (TAT), and usability (survey-based). Secondary endpoints included diagnostic performance of pathologists across both arms and standalone AI against adjudicated reference standard. Analyses included descriptive statistics, paired t-test, and diagnostic performance metrics with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The study included 194 digitized breast biopsies. The mean pathologist overall review time was reduced by 43.5% in DP + AI (40.18 [95% CI: 36.20-44.16] s) versus DP (71.12 [95% CI: 64.39-77.84] s) (p < 0.0001). Diagnostic agreement was 97.42% with DP and 99.48% with DP + AI, with 100% sensitivity observed in the DP + AI workflow. The standalone AI showed high diagnostic accuracy, with area under the curve values ≥0.99 across cancer subtypes. Usability survey showed high satisfaction, ease of use, and perceived clinical utility. Baseline TAT analysis of 3298 cases, independent of study cohort, showed longer TAT for cases requiring immunohistochemistry (IHC; 3.73 days) than for those not requiring (1.17 days). Retrospective workflow modelling suggested that AI-guided IHC pre-ordering could potentially reduce TAT by approximately 2.5 days for patients. DP + AI showed improvements in workflow efficiency while maintaining diagnostic performance. These findings suggest that integration of AI into routine breast pathology workflows may support faster diagnosis, optimized laboratory operations, and improved scalability.

title: Exploratory machine-learning evaluation of clinical and dosimetric features in late prostate radiotherapy toxicity.
summary: Prediction of late radiotherapy toxicity remains challenging, as routinely available clinical and dosimetric variables may incompletely capture individual radiosensitivity. This study evaluated interpretable machine-learning models for predicting baseline- corrected late gastrointestinal (GI) and genitourinary (GU) toxicity following prostate radiotherapy and examined model-derived feature contributions. Data from 229 men with prostate cancer enrolled in the REQUITE cohort were retrospectively analysed. Late toxicity was defined as an increase of ≥1 CTCAE grade from baseline occurring ≥12 months following radiotherapy. Prespecified clinical and dosimetric predictors were evaluated separately for GI and GU toxicity, with correlated dose-volume parameters represented using organ-specific equivalent uniform dose (EUD). L1-regularised logistic regression, Elastic Net and XGBoost were evaluated using repeated nested stratified cross-validation. Performance was assessed using out-of-fold predictions, bootstrap confidence intervals and outcome-label permutation testing. SHAP analysis assessed feature contributions and stability across repeats. GI and GU toxicity worsening occurred in 107 (46.7%) and 125 (54.6%) patients, respectively. GI ROC-AUCs were 0.573, 0.571 and 0.587 for L1, Elastic Net and XGBoost, respectively, with permutation testing indicating above-chance discrimination (p = 0.036, 0.047 and 0.022). Rectal EUD was the most consistently influential GI predictor. GU discrimination was below chance, with no evidence of discrimination beyond the null distribution. GU feature importance was more heterogeneous and model dependent. Routine clinical and dosimetric variables provided limited predictive information for late GI toxicity but did not reliably discriminate GU toxicity. The findings support investigation of additional dosimetric and biological markers for toxicity prediction.

title: Proteomics Reveals Novel Biomarkers in the Blood for Sepsis Diagnosis.
summary: Early sepsis diagnosis in critically ill patients remains a major unmet need. We employed a multiphase proteomic strategy integrating discovery by data-independent acquisition, targeted verification by parallel reaction monitoring, clinical confirmation with ELISA, and machine learning to identify robust blood biomarkers. In discovery and verification cohorts, three consistently downregulated proteins, α-2-HS-glycoprotein (AHSG), clusterin (CLU), and kallistatin (SERPINA4), were prioritized. A random forest model combining these markers yielded an apparent area under the curve (AUC) of 0.94 in the training cohort. Crucially, in a prospective evaluation of 143 patients with suspected sepsis, representing the true test of generalizability, the model achieved an AUC of 0.87, significantly outperforming PCT and CRP, and correctly classified 73.0% of confirmed sepsis cases as high-risk. This triple-biomarker panel enables rapid, accurate early detection of sepsis and offers a readily translatable diagnostic tool for clinical practice.

title: Chronotherapy and Circadian Medicine: Personalizing Treatment Timing with Artificial Intelligence.
summary: This review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming chronotherapy and circadian medicine by enabling precise, individualized estimation of circadian phase. AI algorithms applied to wearable sensors, blood transcriptomes, and multimodal physiologic data now predict internal body times, supporting optimized timing of light therapy, chemotherapy, antiseizure medications, and antihypertensives. While promising applications exist in sleep disorders, oncology, epilepsy, and cardiometabolic conditions, significant barriers remain in data standardization, regulatory approval, and clinical integration. The article highlights recent advances, critically reviews controversial trials (eg, Hygia), and outlines practical steps toward translating AI-guided chronotherapy into routine sleep and medical practice.

title: Mathematical foundations of artificial intelligence in healthcare: a systematic review.
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare relies on diverse mathematical frameworks, yet their contributions to model development, evaluation, interpretability, and clinical translation remain fragmented. This systematic review synthesized the classical and emerging mathematical foundations underpinning healthcare AI and examined major methodological and application trends. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, studies published between January 2016 and June 30, 2026, were identified through systematic searches of Scopus, Google Scholar, and PubMed/MEDLINE, with searches conducted using Harzing's Publish or Perish v8 where applicable. Bibliometric analysis was performed using VOSviewer, while methodological quality was assessed using an adapted JBI-based framework and AMSTAR-2 for systematic reviews. Of 653 records identified, 147 studies met the eligibility criteria. Non-mutually exclusive mathematical-domain coding identified linear algebra in 100/147 studies (68.0%), calculus and optimization in 91/147 (61.9%), and probability and statistics in 79/147 (53.7%), highlighting their roles in data representation, learning, optimization, inference, uncertainty quantification, and validation. A separate mutually exclusive classification of dominant methodological themes identified explainable and trustworthy AI in 24/147 studies (16.3%), statistics and learning theory in 23/147 (15.6%), probability and Bayesian methods in 23/147 (15.6%), calculus and optimization in 19/147 (12.9%), and linear algebra in 15/147 (10.2%). Radiology and medical imaging were the leading healthcare application (24.3%), while classification and diagnosis were the most frequent clinical task (17.1%). Overall, healthcare AI is supported by an interconnected mathematical ecosystem. Emerging approaches, including graph neural networks, Transformers, and quantum machine learning, require stronger external validation, standardized benchmarking, and rigorous evaluation for reliable clinical translation.

title: Better trials, better benchmarks: what clinical AI needs next.
MedGraph: Maintaining Patient State with Graph Memory for Long-Term Medical Dialogue
summary: LLM-based medical assistants that follow a patient across visits need a memory that keeps the patient's clinical state correct as it changes. We examine the errors of five memory systems on longitudinal medical dialogue and find three recurring causes: the retrieved evidence gives an outdated state, includes another person's health facts, or lacks a safety fact the answer depends on. We present MedGraph, a graph memory built for these three cases. Construction extracts dated facts from each session, attributes each fact to the person it describes, and links medication, diagnosis, and measurement records into chains that keep earlier states. Retrieval ranks the patient's chains as units, reads each chain at the time the question asks about, and adds the original dialogue text; a patient profile lists every recorded safety fact with every question. On MedMemoryBench, MedGraph has the highest overall accuracy with both a GPT and a Qwen backbone, 10.5 and 10.4 points above the strongest of five baselines, with efficient memory construction and answering in the GPT setting.

title: Synthesis of Ovarian Cancer Multi-Omics Datasets: A Biology-Informed Evaluation Framework
summary: Paired multi-omic cancer cohorts are costly to assemble and difficult to share, motivating synthetic cohorts as a complementary resource. As generative model development accelerates, we shift the focus from proposing yet another architecture to defining evaluation criteria that determine whether synthetic data preserve biologically relevant structure. We introduce a biology-informed and patient-disjoint framework for evaluating the generation of paired RNA expression and copy-number variation (CNV) profiles, and apply it to the longitudinal DECIDER high-grade serous ovarian cancer cohort. The framework assesses modality-specific fidelity and coherence between RNA and CNV pairs using agreement between real training and held-out data as a reference, alongside complementary training-data proximity diagnostics. We adapt three multi-omic integration architectures based on variational autoencoders to generate paired profiles. The model leading several fidelity and coherence measures also shows the strongest training-data proximity. The protocol and case study offer the community a reference for comparing future multi-omic generators.

title: OraRefer: Segmentation-Guided Multi-Photograph Fusion for Oral Cancer Screening with Guaranteed Patient-Level Sensitivity
summary: Oral cancer and the oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) that can precede it are visible on the oral mucosa, which makes smartphone photographs a promising tool for screening. Deep learning models for this task classify individual photographs. However, screening refers patients, not photographs: a patient is usually photographed several times, and the referral decision must miss no more than a set share of patients with disease. We propose OraRefer, a patient-level screening model that reads each photograph with a segmentation-guided foundation model that conditions its class decision on the predicted lesion, combines all photographs of a patient with risk factors, and refers through a threshold with a finite-sample sensitivity guarantee. The model localizes the mouth itself, so inference needs no annotation. On 3000 photographs of 714 patients, patient-level fusion reaches an AUROC of 0.919 and outperforms attention-based multiple-instance learning. At a 90% sensitivity target, OraRefer detects 95% of patients with OPMD or cancer and misses 3 of 61 patients with cancer, at a specificity of 0.610. Because the threshold is calibrated without retraining, each clinic can set its own guaranteed operating point on a local calibration sample.

title: USB Gym: A Gymnasium Testbed for Closed-Loop Ultrasound View Matching
summary: Background and Objective: Our main goal is ultrasound guidance: moving a probe until its image matches a target view. Published methods for each part of a guide are evaluated in separate simulators. We asked whether these methods, combined into one guide, are good enough. Methods: We built USB Gym, a testbed whose standard engine simulates ultrasound from public patient CT, with a network drawing organ textures from CT labels. Its guide has three replaceable parts (slots), an organ segmenter, a controller and a reward, which received 20 published methods, each run on the same 60 episodes of six held-out patients. In each slot, a published method replaced ours only if detectably better on these patients. The better of this combination and our original guide on 20 new CTs is the benchmark baseline. A pose oracle, reading the exact probe pose available only in simulation, set the reference. The results below are exploratory. Results: On these CTs, the probe started on average 16.0 mm from the target view; the pose oracle brought it to 1.5 mm. Of the results known when the combination was fixed, only an image-similarity reward (SSIM) was slightly but detectably better, so the combination was our guide with that reward. This combination was the benchmark baseline, ending at 13.7 mm (16% of the oracle's progress). Conclusions: Combining untuned published methods with ours did not guide the probe near the target view; the task remains under-explored. The testbed accepts new methods; no guide was tested on hardware.

title: LLM-Assisted Label Noise Correction for EEG-Based Sleep Stage Classification
summary: Automatic sleep stage classification from electroencephalography (EEG) signals is a critical task in clinical sleep medicine. While deep learning models have shown promising results in this domain, their performance is fundamentally constrained by the quality of training labels, which human experts manually annotate and that are subject to inter-rater disagreement and systematic labeling errors. In this paper, we propose a novel LLM-assisted label-noise filtering pipeline that operates exclusively during training to identify and remove unreliable sleep-stage annotations before retraining the classifier. Specifically, TinySleepNet is first trained on the original dataset to extract per-epoch SoftMax confidence scores, then low-confidence epochs are submitted to LLaMA 3.1 along with their EEG spectral features and surrounding sequence context. The LLM evaluates each epoch against AASM sleep-scoring guidelines and assigns a verdict of RELIABLE or SUSPICIOUS. Suspicious epochs are removed from the training set, and TinySleepNet is retrained on the cleaned data. Evaluated on the Sleep-EDF Expanded dataset using 20-fold cross-validation, our method improves overall accuracy from 81.8% to 84.6% and Macro F1-score from 75.6% to 77.4%, with particularly notable gains in REM detection. Crucially, because the LLM operates only during training, the lightweight TinySleepNet architecture (1.3M parameters) is preserved at inference, making the proposed pipeline suitable for real-time, wearable sleep monitoring applications.

title: Transformer-Based Trajectory Prescription for sEMG-Optimizing Robot-Mediated Rehabilitation
summary: Robot-mediated rehabilitation has the potential to deliver high-intensity, individualized therapy, but existing systems (which have not consistently improved outcomes) typically prescribe kinematic trajectories rather than explicitly targeting the neuromotor activations thought to support recovery. To address this gap, and ultimately enable activation-optimizing rehabilitation robot behavior, we present a personalizable transformer-based model mapping individuals' muscle activations (as measured via surface electromyography) to prescribed contact force trajectories when interacting with an end-effector rehabilitation robot. The model uses a transformer encoder-decoder leveraging rotary positional embeddings (RoPE) to generate a latent representation of trajectory-relevant and user-specific neuromotor factors, and augments trajectory prediction with flow matching to produce a distribution over plausible prescriptions biased toward the training distribution. Using data from 16 healthy participants completing 15 isometric trajectory tracking tasks, we evaluate generalization across held-out tasks and users, as well as the feasibility of user-specific fine-tuning within a therapy-session timescale. The model achieves mean trajectory prediction errors of <8% on held out tasks and users, with effectively instantaneous deterministic inference and sub-second sampling of trajectory distributions. An initial test using the model during live rehabilitation tasks demonstrates that, on average, participants reach the target neuromotor activations with just 15% error accumulated throughout the task. These results provide a proof of concept for data-driven, activation-targeted trajectory prescription in robot-mediated rehabilitation and establish a foundation for future validation in clinical populations. Data and code have been open-sourced as part of the OpenRobotRehab project on SimTK.

title: Multimodal Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts for 3D Medical Vision-Language Modeling
summary: Medical 3D scans and reports are inherently hierarchical, with diagnostic cues concentrated in specific anatomical regions across multiple levels of organization. Yet, most medical vision-language models ignore this structure and fail to focus on clinically relevant anatomy. We introduce MedHiVE, which combines hierarchical vision-language Soft Mixture-of-Experts (SMoE) with contrastive learning to jointly model fine-grained anatomy and global scan context. To our knowledge, MedHiVE is the first framework to route both vision and text tokens through a two-level SMoE hierarchy organized by anatomical scale, coupling this with report-derived anatomy-level contrastive alignment for 3D medical imaging. This replaces the direct region-text alignment of statically pooled features and vision-only hierarchical routing of prior work with dynamic, slot-based cross-modal information flow across anatomical scales. MedHiVE operates via a two-level, learnable token-routing mechanism, where local image and text features are first routed through a local SMoE and then fused by a global SMoE into unified multimodal representations. Contrastive learning aligns both anatomy-level and global vision-language representations in a unified space. Pre-trained on 25,000+ CT scans with anatomical supervision, MedHiVE consistently surpasses 11 state-of-the-art methods across 6 datasets on 3 tasks: segmentation, classification, and detection, demonstrating the importance of hierarchical modeling. The code for MedHiVE is at github.com/szczurek-lab/MedHiVE.

title: Interpretable Multimodal MRI-Clinical Fusion for Functional Outcome Prediction After Acute Ischemic Stroke
summary: This study evaluates the added prognostic value of day-1 multimodal MRI for predicting three-month functional outcome after acute ischemic stroke (AIS). Sixty-six AIS patients with ADC, DWI, FLAIR, and clinical data were analyzed. Three-dimensional pretrained ResNet embeddings were extracted from each MRI modality, reduced using fold-isolated principal component analysis, and combined with structured clinical variables and ADC-derived lesion biomarkers. Linear support vector machines were evaluated using eight-fold stratified group cross-validation across MRI modality combinations. Clinical-only modeling achieved strong performance (AUC = $0.899 \pm 0.151$), while MRI-only models showed limited discrimination (AUC $\approx$ $0.67$-$0.73$). Among multimodal configurations, FLAIR-clinical fusion achieved the highest mean cross-validated performance (AUC = $0.948 \pm 0.061$), followed by ADC-clinical fusion (AUC = $0.941 \pm 0.094$). Full ADC-DWI-FLAIR fusion did not consistently outperform single-modality clinical fusion. Feature-importance analysis identified age, NIHSS subscores, ADC lesion burden, and learned FLAIR representations as key contributors, while qualitative FLAIR activation maps showed responses over lesion-like regions. These findings suggest that compact day-1 FLAIR and ADC representations provide complementary prognostic information beyond clinical variables and support interpretable, data-efficient outcome prediction in AIS.

title: ProtoGestalt: Interpretable Prototypes for Facial Phenotyping and Diagnosis of Rare Genetic Disorders
summary: Rare genetic disorders are difficult to diagnose due to their diversity and overlapping clinical features. Facial morphology can provide diagnostic clues, yet most diagnostic models offer limited interpretability and are not designed to support broad screening for undiagnosed disease. We present ProtoGestalt, an interpretable prototype-based framework for facial phenotyping, rare-disease screening, and syndrome identification. The method extends prototype learning by constraining learned visual features to select facial regions, allowing predictions to be explained through localized and additive evidence. We assess ProtoGestalt's ability to distinguish syndromic from unaffected faces on multiple control datasets and class prevalence values. We further evaluate it's diagnostic performance on syndromes observed during training. The learned prototype-based representations provide significant separation between syndromic and case-matched control images and retain useful performance as the proportion of controls increases. The framework also demonstrates the ability to differentiate among syndromes. Although reasonably accurate specialized models for facial classification of rare disorders already exist, ProtoGestalt offers an interpretable alternative that links predictions to anatomically meaningful facial regions, potentially supporting clinical decision-making and the discovery of phenotype-gene associations.

title: GTAFL: Addressing Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning in Medical Image
summary: In healthcare, protecting patient privacy is crucial due to the sensitivity of medical data and its extensive accessibility. Federated Learning (FL) offers a decentralized and privacy-preserving training paradigm, making it an ideal solution for healthcare applications. A critical challenge in healthcare is that real-world medical data often exhibits long-tailed distributions in local and global views. Existing methods addressing long-tailed FL problem typically assume that the model will be evaluated on uniform test data distribution. However, practical test data in healthcare systems is often agnostic and unpredictable, leading to potential model failures in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we introduce a novel task termed Test-Agnostic Long-Tailed Federated Learning and propose GTAFL, a comprehensive framework to address this challenge. During the training stage, GTAFL employs adaptive re-sampling, expert classifier retraining, and self-supervised learning to correct biased classifiers and distorted feature spaces caused by long-tailed training distributions.
