title: Multi-BOUNTI: Multi-lobe Brain vOlUmetry and segmeNtation for feTal and neonatal MRI
summary: Regional volumetric assessment of perinatal brain development is currently limited by the lack of consistent high quality multi-regional fast segmentation methods applicable to both fetal and neonatal MRI. We present Multi-BOUNTI, a deep learning pipeline for automated multi-lobe segmentation of fetal and neonatal T2w brain MRI. The method is based on a dedicated 43-label parcellation protocol and a 3D Attention U-Net trained on brain MRI datasets of subjects spanning 21-44 weeks gestational/postmenstrual age. The pipeline integrates preprocessing, segmentation and volumetric analysis, and was evaluated on independent datasets, demonstrating fast (<10 min/case) and accurate performance with high agreement to manually refined labels. We demonstrate the application of the framework with 267 fetal and 593 neonatal MRI datasets from the developing Human Connectome Project without reported clinically significant brain anomalies to derive normative volumetric growth models across 21-44 weeks GA/PMA. These models were used to characterise developmental trajectories, assess differences between fetal and preterm neonatal cohorts, and analyse longitudinal changes. The resulting normative models were integrated into an automated reporting framework enabling subject-specific volumetric assessment via centiles and z-scores. Multi-BOUNTI provides a unified and scalable approach for perinatal brain segmentation and volumetry, supporting large-scale studies and facilitating future clinical translation. The full pipeline is publicly available at https://github.com/SVRTK/perinatal-brain-mri-analysis.

title: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19
summary: Predicting the progression of COVID-19 in hospitalised patients was an important challenge during the pandemic, particularly when healthcare resources were limited. This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models to predict three clinical outcomes: death, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and clinical status (improvement or worsening). The study uses two patient datasets: an Algerian cohort of 80 patients from the Internal Medicine Department of the University Hospital Centre of Constantine, collected between July and August 2020, and a French cohort of 99 patients collected between March and May 2020. Five ML classifiers were evaluated: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), classification and regression trees (CART), Naive Bayes (NB), and support vector machines (SVM). Their performance was examined in combination with three feature-selection methods: analysis of variance (ANOVA), mutual information (MI), and recursive feature elimination (RFE). The results were also compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using one to five hidden layers. Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

title: Similar discrimination, different behaviour under synthetic occlusion: confidence and attribution reproducibility of deep learning models for intraoral ultrasonography
summary: Objectives: To determine whether similar baseline discrimination conceals different responses to synthetic occlusion, whether loss of discrimination is accompanied by reduced confidence, and whether spatial attributions are reproducible in intraoral ultrasonography models. Methods: We analysed 477 images from 40 healthy volunteers, using acquisition position to label superior and inferior subregions. Five architectures were evaluated across five training seeds on a subject-independent test set of 97 images from eight volunteers. Images underwent constant-intensity occlusion at boundaries spanning 30-70% of image depth and an area-matched band-occlusion control. Attribution analyses assessed variation across seeds and class-activation methods and compared attribution-guided insertion with random insertion. Results: Seed-mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.958 to 0.972, with rankings reversing across seeds. EfficientNet-B0 fell below 0.60 in 49 of 50 boundary-sweep conditions, compared with zero to two for the other architectures; the difference persisted with area-matched masking. Under 50% occlusion, its mean confidence on incorrect predictions rose to 0.989 and expected calibration error from 0.094 to 0.478. Between two inference runs, EfficientNet-B0's per-seed occluded AUCs differed by up to 0.161; seed means were 0.51-0.55 in both. Attribution patterns varied across seeds and methods.

title: Prospective In-silico Simulation of the VESALIUS-CV Trial Using Biomedical Knowledge Graph and Real-World Data-Driven AI Modeling
summary: Cardiovascular outcomes trials are lengthy and costly. In silico trial simulation using real-world data may support earlier decision-making, but evidence generated before trial results are disclosed remains limited. We applied a semi-mechanistic machine learning framework integrating patient-level real-world data with knowledge graph-derived drug representations to simulate the VESALIUS-CV trial of evolocumab versus placebo before its results were public, using a locked model and prespecified trial design aligned with the trial protocol. Patient-level time-to-event predictions were aggregated into virtual trial arms to estimate cumulative incidence, hazard ratios (HR), confidence intervals (CI), and p-values for three-point major adverse cardiovascular events. In retrospective evaluation of the model's patient-level predictive performance, time-dependent areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.80 to 0.90 across follow-up horizons. In evaluation of retrospective trial-level predictive performance across 22 cardiovascular trials, the model predicted trial meeting the primary outcome with an accuracy of 0.91 (95% CI 0.77-1) and F1 score of 0.95 (95%CI 0.86-1). The prospective simulation predicted a significant reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events with evolocumab (HR 0.78; 95%CI, 0.70 to 0.87) at 54 months. The trial subsequently reported a HR of 0.75 (95% confidence interval, 0.65 to 0.86) at a median follow-up of 55 months, with progressive separation of event curves in both the simulation and the trial. The prospective simulation was concordant with the direction, magnitude, and temporal dynamics of the observed treatment effect, supporting in silico simulation as a tool for early decision-making, trial design, and de-risking in cardiovascular drug development.

title: Deep learning screening of otoscopic images for ENT referral: development, validation and deployment of NHREF OtoScan
summary: Background. Middle and external ear disease is common and largely treatable, but accurate otoscopic interpretation requires training that is scarce outside specialist ENT services. Published deep learning models for otoscopy report high accuracy, yet most are optimised for closed set classification rather than the referral decision a non specialist actually makes, report uncalibrated probabilities, and do not report the near duplicate controls that video derived otoscopic datasets demand. We developed, validated and deployed a screening aid framed around referral rather than diagnosis. Methods. We merged 4,763 otoscopic images from 16 folders across three public datasets into 12 clinically meaningful classes. Every image was passed through a single field of view normalisation function (crop to the illuminated field, square, resize to 224 px, mask to one fixed circle) shared identically by training and inference, to remove the framing cue that otherwise identifies the source dataset. Because one source is video derived, images were grouped by cosine similarity of generic ImageNet features (threshold 0.93, joined transitively) and whole groups assigned to a single split, giving 3,326 training, 719 validation and 718 test images. A MobileNetV2 backbone initialised from ImageNet was fine tuned from block9expand. Probabilities were averaged over the eight dihedral transforms of each image and temperature scaled. The referral score was one minus the probability of a normal ear, and its threshold was set on the validation abnormal ears as the highest value still meeting a target sensitivity of 97%, applied with an inclusive comparison. Model selection, calibration and threshold were frozen before the test split was scored once. Results. On the 718 held out test images, referral sensitivity was 97.0% (95% CI 95.1 to 98.2) and specificity 75.6% (95% CI 69.4 to 80.8), with AUROC 0.974 for abnormal versus normal; a cluster bootstrap over the 363 similarity groups in the test split widens those intervals to 93.8 99.6% and 66.0 83.4% respectively. Of 501 abnormal ears, 15 were not referred; 11 of these were myringosclerosis and none was cholesteatoma. Twelve class macro F1 was 0.686, balanced accuracy 68.3%, and accuracy 85.0% (86.2% with chronic subtypes merged). Temperature scaling (T = 1.2) reduced expected calibration error from 0.0498 to 0.0430. A low confidence flag fired on 4.0% of test images, separating 87.2% accuracy on unflagged from 31.0% on flagged cases. Recall was consistently highest on the largest source dataset and fell on the other two, for example acute otitis media 95.5% on source A versus 50.0% on source B. Conclusions. A compact, calibrated model run on ordinary CPU hardware achieved the pre specified 97% referral sensitivity with clinically interpretable failure modes. The source stratified gap, and an earlier perceptual hash split that inflated scores until it was corrected, indicate that headline accuracy in this field is strongly dependent on leakage control and acquisition style. The system is deployed with mandatory specialist review, a daily backtest and approval gated retraining, so that prospective performance on local equipment is measured rather than assumed. It is research software and not a medical device.

title: Large Language Model-Enhanced Electronic Frailty Assessment and Prognostic Performance in Hospitalized Adults: A Retrospective Cohort Study
summary: Background: Electronic frailty indices (eFIs) derived from structured electronic health record (EHR) data may incompletely capture functional deficits. Large language models (LLMs) can extract frailty-related information from clinical notes, but whether improved frailty ascertainment improves prognostic performance is uncertain. Objective: To compare frailty ascertainment and prognostic performance between standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs among hospitalized adults. Design: Retrospective cohort study Participants: Adults aged 50 years or older enrolled in two studies at an academic medical center and affiliated community hospital between February 2022 and April 2024. Main Measures: A validated 35-deficit diagnosis-based eFI and an LLM-enhanced eFI incorporating deficits extracted from physical therapy (PT) documentation using GPT-4o. Frailty was defined using an index threshold of 0.20 or more. The primary outcome was a composite of discharge to a facility, readmission, or death within 90 days. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed associations with the outcome, and discrimination was compared using area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Secondary analyses examined threshold-based classification and PT-documentation availability; prespecified sensitivity analyses evaluated population and outcome restrictions. Results: Among 616 hospitalizations, mean (SD) age was 70.9 (10.2) years, 329 (53.4%) had PT documentation, and 320 (51.9%) experienced the composite outcome. Standard and LLM-enhanced eFIs classified 216 (35.1%) and 362 (58.8%) hospitalizations as frail, respectively. Both were independently associated with the outcome (standard eFI: adjusted OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.39-2.83]; LLM-enhanced eFI: adjusted OR, 2.46 [95% CI, 1.75-3.47]). Discrimination did not differ significantly (AUROC, 0.636 vs 0.660; difference, 0.024 [95% CI, -0.006 to 0.053]; p=0.12). LLM enhancement increased sensitivity (42.5% to 69.4%) but decreased specificity (73.0% to 52.7%). Conclusions: LLM enhancement substantially increased frailty ascertainment and sensitivity for adverse outcomes but did not significantly improve prognostic discrimination. Thus, LLM-enhanced frailty assessment may depend on whether the intended use prioritizes broad identification of functional vulnerability or prediction of adverse post-hospital outcomes.

title: Uncovering Distinct Phenotypes of Early Onset Heart Failure in Women
summary:
BackgroundHeart failure in younger women is understudied and may reflect heterogeneous pathways and risk not adequately captured by conventional classifications. We aimed to identify clinically distinct phenotypes of early-onset heart failure in women, assess their prognostic significance, and evaluate their transportability in an independent national cohort.

MethodsWe identified women aged 18-55 years with heart failure using electronic health record data from a large multi-hospital system. A variational deep embedding model incorporating 283 clinical features was used for unsupervised phenotyping. Associations with subsequent inpatient hospitalization, emergency department utilization, and mortality were evaluated using age-stratified Cox models. Phenotype transportability was assessed by both applying the institutionally trained model and by independent de novo clustering as a replication analysis in the All of Us cohort.

ResultsAmong 1,407 young women with heart failure (median age, 45 years), four phenotypes were identified: hypertensive pregnancy (n=494), cardiorenal (n=276), autoimmune (n=394), and cardiometabolic-ischemic (n=243), with a bootstrap adjusted Rand index of 0.65 and silhouette score of 0.45. Compared with the hypertensive pregnancy phenotype, risks of inpatient hospitalization were highest for the cardiorenal (HR 2.86 [95% CI, 2.35-3.49]) and autoimmune (HR 2.25 [95% CI, 1.87-2.70]) phenotypes; mortality risks were similarly elevated (HR 4.65 [95% CI, 3.17-6.82] and HR 4.38 [95% CI, 3.03-6.31], respectively) in these two groups. In All of Us participants (n=682), transferred phenotypes retained their principal clinical characteristics and continued to stratify hospitalization risk. Independent clustering most strongly reproduced the cardiorenal phenotype (Jaccard index, 0.744).

ConclusionsEarly-onset heart failure in women comprises distinct cardio-obstetric, cardiorenal, autoimmune, and cardiometabolic-ischemic phenotypes with divergent clinical outcomes. These findings support a life-course approach to heart failure classification in women that complements conventional frameworks and incorporates pregnancy history and female-predominant systemic conditions.

Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSUnsupervised machine learning identifies distinct clinical phenotypes of heart failure among young women, highlighting heterogeneity in a population that remains understudied.
These phenotypes captured differing cardiometabolic, cardiovascular, and pregnancy-related characteristics, suggesting potentially distinct pathways contributing to heart failure development.
External validation in the All of Us cohort supported external validity and demonstrated the potential for identifying these patterns across diverse healthcare populations.


What Are the Clinical Implications?Heart failure in young women is clinically diverse, underscoring the importance of comprehensive assessment beyond traditional heart failure classifications, including cardiometabolic risk factors and pregnancy history.
Recognition of distinct clinical phenotypes may help clinicians identify women with differing risk profiles and inform more individualized approaches to cardiovascular evaluation, risk factor management, and longitudinal follow-up.
Further studies are needed to determine whether phenotypes differ in treatment responses and whether phenotype-guided management can improve outcomes.

title: A scalable invariant causal discovery framework reveals direct genetic and clinical determinants of complex human traits
summary: Identifying genetic and clinical factors that exert direct causal effects on complex traits is central to precision medicine, yet remains a major challenge. Association-based methods cannot distinguish cause from consequence, and existing causal frameworks are limited by stringent assumptions or computational intractability in high-dimensional settings. Invariant causal prediction (ICP) offers a principled alternative but has seen minimal application in genetic epidemiology due to exponential complexity. Here, we introduce the Invariant Generalized Covariance Measure (I-GCM), a scalable framework that integrates ICP principles with machine learning to identify direct causal variables. I-GCM combines PC-simple screening with a generalized covariance measure (GCM) computed via gradient-boosted trees to test invariance across environments, capturing both linear and nonlinear dependencies. In simulations (up to 3,000 variables, 50,000 samples), I-GCM achieved PPV of approximately 0.84-1.00 and specificity >=0.99, outperforming PC-simple by 0.21-0.29 in precision with comparable sensitivity. Applying I-GCM to the UK Biobank, we identified direct causal genes and clinical risk factors for COVID-19 susceptibility and severity and for HDL and triglyceride levels, with many findings supported by existing literature and pathway enrichment. Notably, JAK1 was identified as a direct causal gene for severe COVID-19, consistent with clinical use of the JAK1-targeting therapy baricitinib. To our knowledge, this is among the first applications of invariance-based causal discovery to genetic epidemiology at a biobank scale. By bridging statistical causality and translational medicine, I-GCM offers a scalable, interpretable, and high-precision framework for mechanistic discovery and therapeutic target prioritization.

title: Divergent Causes of Death After Ischemic and Hemorrhagic Stroke in the Reperfusion Era: A Contemporary Cohort Study
summary: Background: Contemporary data on long-term, cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors are sparse, and much of the existing evidence derives from studies performed before the modern reperfusion era. We sought to characterize long-term cause-specific mortality among stroke survivors to discharge (differentiated by stroke subtype) when compared to in-hospital stroke decedents treated under contemporary standards of care. Methods: Using a hybrid billing-code/imaging and large language model-assisted chart-review pipeline, we identified adults hospitalized for ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in the Observational Study of Cardiac Arrest Risk (OSCAR) cohort (Cedars-Sinai Health System, Los Angeles) between 2017 and 2020, followed through June 30, 2025. Cause of death was determined and classified into 10 categories. Results: Among 1,344 stroke patients (mean age 74.0 {+/-} 14.9 years; ischemic n=1,036 [77.1%], hemorrhagic n=308 [22.9%]), 203 (15.1%) did not survive the index stroke. Of the 1,141 discharged survivors, 625 (54.8%) died over a median follow-up of 5.2 years. Cerebrovascular causes predominated during index stroke hospitalization (36.0%) but accounted for only 15.5% of post-stroke discharge deaths. Among ischemic stroke survivors, cardiac disease was the leading cause of death (31.6%), with sudden cardiac arrest alone accounting for 10.9% of deaths. Among hemorrhagic stroke survivors, cancer (38.9%) was the leading cause of death. Despite these divergent cause-of-death profiles, overall survival did not differ significantly by subtype (median 5.5 vs 5.8 years; P=0.90). Conclusions: In this contemporary, reperfusion-era cohort, causes of death shifted from cerebrovascular predominance in the acute phase to heart disease/cardiac arrest after ischemic stroke, and malignancy after hemorrhagic stroke. These findings argue for development of subtype-specific post-stroke surveillance, including structured longitudinal cardiac and sudden-death risk assessment for ischemic stroke survivors.

title: Role Of Innate Immunity to NeuroHIV in the cART Era
summary:
PROJECT SUMMARY
 A significant percentage of people living with HIV/AIDS (PLWHA) exhibit HIV associated neurocognitive
disorders (HAND). With the development and improvement of combination antiretroviral therapies (cART) there
was a substantial decrease of the death and morbidity rates of PLWHA. Despite the cART progress, PLWHA
still present a high prevalence as chronic neuroinflammation, where the cellular mechanism(s) that drive such
inflammation have not been entirely defined.
 Certain models of neuroinflammation define inter-cellular cytokine signalling as a major player in
neuroinflammation. These models propose that activation of microglia results in the production of inflammatory
cytokines and metabolites (e.g. IL-1α, TNFα, IL-6, C1q) that are recognized by astrocytes, leading to a
modification from non-reactive astrocytes to a range of pro-inflammatory or repair phenotypes. In this proposal
we aim to identify the molecular mechanisms that trigger the activation of intracellular innate immunity in
microglia, as well to characterize the cellular crosstalk between HIV infected and non-infected cells in the brain
under physiological concentrations of cART.
 Our preliminary data from gene expression and viral interaction with innate sensing immune complexes points
to an activation of the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)/stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway in
microglia under cART. Thus, we hypothesize that the activation of the cGAS/STING pathway leads to episodes
of chronic neuroinflamation in the context of HIV and cART therapy . We will determine the impact of cART on
HIV cytoplasmic trafficking and the activation of innate immune sensing. We will characterize the biologic
consequences to HIV-mediated innate sensing in astrocytes and neurons under brain physiologic cART
concentrations. We will carry out an experimental plan to characterize the impact of activation of the
cGAS/STING in the brain with funcional assays, cyclic multiplex immunofluorescence and super-resolution
fluorescence imaging, machine learning analysis, single cell and bulk RNAseq, and multiplexed cytokine profiling
in iPSC-derived microglia and cerebral brain organoids.
 These studies will define the activation of HIV mediated innate immunity in cells from the brain that are known
to be infected by HIV and the impact of this activation in the disruption of normal brain homeostasis by
inflammatory processes. At the heart of this proposal is the clarification and identification of the
mechanism(s) that drive and/or contribute to persistent neuroinflammation under cART that culminate
in HAND. Knowledge gained from this research plan can inform therapeutic potential to ameliorate
and/or reduce HAND in PLWHA.

title: Multi-target repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) treatment for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and comorbid pain
summary:
PROJECT SUMMARY
Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and fibromyalgia (FM) are highly comorbid, disabling and resistant to
treatment. More than half of MDD patients present with pain symptoms, and the comorbidity is associated with
reduced quality of life, poor pharmacological treatment outcomes, and opioid use disorders. New approaches to
help comorbid patients are urgently needed. Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) treatment may
ameliorate both pain and mood symptoms, possibly through modulation of shared underlying pathophysiological
brain networks.
Preliminary data indicate rTMS applied to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lDLPFC) significantly improved
both depressive and moderate pain symptoms but failed to improve more severe comorbid pain. In this
application, we propose to test the efficacy of a multi-target rTMS protocol that may be more successful in treating
both mood and pain symptoms in comorbid MDD/FM. This includes two complementary objectives: 1) to test the
effects of a novel rTMS protocol for comorbid MDD and FM, and 2) to provide critical additional training to the
candidate that will facilitate her transition into independence as a researcher specializing in the comorbidity of
mood disorders with chronic pain and their treatment with rTMS. This will be achieved through a randomized,
sham-controlled study with two experimental conditions: A) Active rTMS to lDLPFC (established target for MDD)
and sham rTMS to the primary motor cortex (M1, established pain target); and B) Active rTMS to both, lDLPFC
and M1. We anticipate that multi-site rTMS will be more efficacious to treat both MDD and FM symptoms than
the single site rTMS protocol. Additionally, we will determine the differences and similarities of neural signatures
of MDD and FM and how these interact in the comorbid condition using machine learning techniques.
The K01 project will take place at UCLA with the mentoring support from the director of the Neuromodulation
Division, two co-mentors and four other collaborators with expertise in rTMS, depression, chronic pain,
multimodal imaging, and machine learning analysis. This approach will achieve the project’s specific aims to: 1.
Evaluate the effect of multi-site vs. single site rTMS on clinical symptoms; 2. Determine the interaction of
networks affected in MDD and chronic pain and how they are modulated by rTMS; and 3. Examine the interaction
between analgesic and antidepressant effects of rTMS. If these aims are achieved, the short-term outcome of
this project will help determine the efficacy of multi-site rTMS for comorbid MDD and FM, identify the overlap of
the neural signature of MDD and FM and how it is modulated by rTMS, and characterize the relationship between
rTMS-induced antidepressant and analgesic effects. In the long-term, current rTMS procedures may be
significantly improved for the treatment of MDD with comorbid chronic pain.

title: Cerebral Small Vessel Disease and Dementia: Defining Global Resilience and Disruption in Brain Networks
summary: My goal is to establish myself as an independent biomedical researcher in brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and AD related dementias (ADRD). My passion to build a career in aging stems from my profound desire to help older people to maintain their functionality and quality of life. AD/ADRD are particularly interesting to me due their complex heterogeneous nature and my enthusiasm to work on complex health problems. The Wake Forest School of Medicine provides an exceptional environment to build a career in this field as it’s a nationally recognized leader in geriatric research with multiple NIH-funded P30 centers (P30AG072947 ADRC and P30 Pepper OAIC) focused on aging process and age-related disorders. The K25 Mentored Career Development Award will provide a unique opportunity for me to build a rigorous foundation in this new direction by leveraging the didactic research and training opportunities offered by this environment. I have briefly described my research and training objectives for this award. Research. The most common form of neuropathology in older adults is mixed cerebral small vessel disease and AD pathologies. Despite this, we have major gaps in our practical understanding of small vessel disease contribution to cognitive dysfunction and decline. Specifically, the impacts of small vessel disease on brain networks are largely unknown. In my K25 application, by focusing on cerebral microbleeds (CMB), as common manifestations of small vessel disease, I seek to address this critical gap. My specific aims are to: 1) utilize advanced brain network modeling to uncover and quantify network resilience/disruption from CMB, 2) use an integrative machine learning model with novel brain network biomarkers of CMB to improve predicting cognitive impairment, and 3) develop and deploy software packages to disseminate the developed methods that enable researchers to ask similar questions with other biomarkers of neuropathology and verify findings of this study. My proposed research can provide novel tools and insights to enable a translational shift in our practical understanding of mechanistic impacts of CMB on the brain to allow incorporating them into current diagnostic and treatment frameworks. Training. My specific training objectives for the protected time provided by this award are to: 1) establish knowledge of healthy and abnormal aging within the context of AD/ADRD, 2) gain expertise in the vascular contributions to AD/ADRD, 3) acquire in-depth knowledge about imaging biomarkers of small vessel disease, and 4) improve collaborative research, networking, and grant writing skills. I will be guided by an outstanding team of multidisciplinary clinicians and scholars in aging and AD/ADRD, neuroscience, and statistics to accomplish these objectives through attending courses, conferences, seminars, workshops, and shadowing geriatric clinicians and neuroradiologists. The preliminary work from this study will open opportunities to study the effect of small vessel disease and other age-related pathology on brain health and risk for AD/ADRD and preclinical results for future R01 submissions.

title: Personalizing Veterans' Lung Cancer Screening and Diagnosis
summary:
Personalizing Veteran's Lung Cancer Screening and Diagnosis
Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-specific mortality in United States, including among Veterans. Annual
lung cancer screening with low-dose chest computed tomography (LDCT) in high-risk individuals has been
demonstrated to save lives in two large, randomized-controlled trials and is recommended by the US Preventive
Services Task Force (USPSTF) for individuals aged 50 to 80 with at least 20 pack years of smoking and who
currently smoke or quit in the past 15 years. Yet, individuals eligible under these criteria would only capture 45-
65% of all lung cancers. In this proposal, we seek to personalize lung cancer screening and diagnosis.
Veterans are at great risk for lung cancer given the higher prevalence of tobacco smoking and service-connected
exposures, including agent orange, asbestos, burn pits, and ionizing radiation. These hazardous materials and
exposures, frequently encountered in the military, are associated with lung cancer but are not part of current
recommended eligibility criteria. Furthermore, lung cancer screening results in an increase in the detection of
indeterminant pulmonary nodules. Our teams' data suggests that two candidate biomarkers could mitigate
sending Veterans with benign nodules for invasive procedures and shorten the time to lung cancer diagnosis.
First, an artificial intelligence model (Lung Cancer Predictor Convolutional Neural Network, LCP-CNN)
significantly improves discrimination between benign and malignant nodules on LDCTs. Our LCP-CNN algorithm
generates accurate reclassification of up to 30% of intermediate risk nodules (10-70% risk for cancer) to lower
or higher risk levels, thus, decreasing the number of invasive procedures and shortening the time to diagnosis.
The other biomarker is CYFRA 21-1, a serum protein cancer biomarker for which we developed a high sensitivity
assay. Based on these preliminary data, we propose to answer the following clinical question: Can we safely
offer lung cancer screening to Veterans who are at greater risk beyond their age and smoking history
but due to their personal and service-related exposures while improving the rate of early and non-
invasive detection of lung cancer?
Aim 1: In a prospective cohort of 800 Veterans at Nashville, Denver and Louisville between 50-80 years of age
who ever smoked cigarettes, we will evaluate if a new, personalized lung cancer screening eligibility criteria that
incorporates military exposures, COPD, personal history of tobacco-related cancer, and family history of lung
cancer results in at least the same number of lung cancers detected compared to the standard of care USPSTF
screening criteria in use by our Lung Precision Oncology Program lung cancer screening programs.
Aim 2: Among a cohort of Nashville Veterans with positive screenings (n=520), we will test the hypothesis that
the LCP-CNN in combination with hs-CYFRA 21-1 reduces the number of invasive procedures and shortens the
time to lung cancer diagnosis versus the Brock Model. We will manage positive screens from Aim 1 and test the
combined biomarker approach proposed in Aim 2 to rule in cancer early and rule out benign lung nodules.
Impact: We will safely personalize lung cancer screening in the Veteran community to improve the number of
cancers detected early, reduce the rate of invasive procedures, and avoid a missed chance for cure for early
detected lung cancers. This project will provide proof of principle for personalizing lung cancer screening criteria
among Veterans and test the clinical utility of a combined biomarker-based approach to manage screen-detected
indeterminate pulmonary nodules. The proposed research will provide actionable evidence for Veterans with
military exposures and would impact VHA policy. Our team is poised to conduct a rigorous and necessary
evaluation and the findings will inform the development of a larger, national randomized-controlled CSP trial to
test if LDCT screening among Veterans meeting expanded and personalized criteria results in improved survival.

title: Augmenting the VA NAFLD Dashboard with Dynamic Random Forest Models
summary:
Significance to VA: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a significant and growing health problem
closely linked with the metabolic syndrome (obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, and
dyslipidemia). Untreated, NAFLD can lead to life threatening and costly cirrhosis, liver cancer, and the need
for a liver transplant. In the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), NAFLD prevalence has been estimated
to be as high as 46%. Up to 20% of the VA NAFLD population can progress to fibrosis/cirrhosis. In the Dallas
Heart Study, the highest prevalence of NAFLD occurred among Hispanics (58%), and those with T2DM (over
70%). Importantly, the current economic burden of NAFLD results in estimated liver-related costs in the
billions annually in the VA. Current tools are suboptimal in accurately differentiating patients with NAFLD at
low and high risk to advanced disease stages (nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), fibrosis, and cirrhosis).
Thus, low risk patients are unnecessarily referred for treatment (e.g., 35% of patients at the Charleston VA
NAFLD Clinic in 2017 and 48% at the Richmond VA Medical Center in 2017-2019), while those that are at
high risk of progression are often under recognized and not referred for treatment. Building upon our previous
models predicting mortality among patients meeting the Husain criteria for NAFLD, we will extend the
predictive models to liver disease and the metabolic syndrome and augment dynamic dashboards to support
hepatologists and primary care physicians in making referrals of Veterans at high risk of progression.
Innovation & Impact: This project will provide innovative information to improve our understanding of NAFLD
and metabolic syndrome progression and assist in referring patients at high risk of progression to NAFLD
specialty clinics. The study uses an innovative conceptual framework to support health system research. The
framework is based on systems thinking and the success of clinical microsystems in healthcare. Here we
incorporate system thinking approaches for steatotic liver disease and metabolic syndrome population health.
The information management system can be used to inform policy decisions and clinical practices for
treatment of liver disease and the metabolic syndrome.
Specific Aims: Aim 1. Replicate extant Random Forest (RF) models as well as extend RF models developed
in our HSR&D pilot study for early prediction of NAFLD progression and mortality. We will compare
predictions of models with non-invasive NFS, FIB-4, and Fibroscan over a 5-year and 10-year interval after
first identification of NAFLD by Husain criteria and measure NAFLD progression (cirrhosis, cirrhosis-related
complications, fibrosis), CVD events and mortality. Aim 2. Expand the RF models to be both temporal and
incremental so they incorporate metabolic severity Z-score to predict MASLD progression, CVD events, and
mortality in 5- and 10-year interval after MASLD first identification compared with non-invasive measure NFS,
FIB-4, and Fibroscan. Aim 3. Compare Systems Usability Scale (SUS) ratings and accuracy of referrals to
specialty clinics for the two types of NAFLD Dashboards (tabular, dynamic with RF models) as well as collect
user perceptions of facilitators and barriers.
Methodology: We will replicate extant RF models and extend our RF predictive analytic approaches to
incorporate temporal information and incrementally add new information to identify patients with higher risk of
cirrhosis, cirrhosis-related complications, cardiovascular events, and mortality with a focused analysis on
racial, ethnicity and rurality disparities. We will assess dynamic dashboards for referral using the models.
Path to Translation/Implementation: Machine Learning predictive models built using variables from
Veterans with NAFLD or metabolic syndrome, will result in models utilized in dynamic dashboards that identify
high risk subgroups and improve referrals of Veterans at high risk of progression.

title: Mechanism-based serum biomarkers and validation of ensemble model for excessive alcohol use
summary:
Project Summary
Increasing the sensitivity and specificity of biomarkers for recognizing recent, excessive alcohol use (EAU) in
Veterans is a timely goal of research. EAU is becoming recognized as an emerging health-related problem
especially among veterans returning from combats. As such, there is a need for increased vigilance and action
to identify and counsel at-risk veterans. The diagnosis and care of veteran patients with EAU is hampered by
the lack of tests with high diagnostic performance that can detect dangerous levels of drinking or relapse
during therapy. Such tests would be indispensable for screening and care for veterans with EAU. The
consequences of under-detection of EAU, thus delayed intervention are serious because relative risk of alcohol-
related health conditions is increased with the amounts and duration of alcohol consumed per day. Excessive
alcohol use (EAU) is becoming recognized as an emerging health-related problem especially among veterans
returning from combats. Our preliminary data using the new landscape of proteomic and transcriptomic
approaches have uncovered the pathophysiology of EAU on several pathways; which might lead to
pathology in human. This renewal CSR&D Merit Review Award application seeks the support to define
the roles of the panels of biomarkers; derived from the effect of EAU on inflammatory response to screen
for EAU and quantity of recent alcohol consumption and monitoring for abstinence. We hypothesize that
(i) these biomarkers derived from system biology analyses are useful and have a better diagnostic performance
to screen for EAU and the quantity of recent alcohol consumption in clinical practice, when compared to the
conventional markers and (ii) the combination of these markers into a single risk model prediction using
machine learning and statistical mechanics will revolutionize the way we screen for EAU in clinical practice. To
test this hypothesis, we plan to pursue the following specific aims; SPECIFIC AIM # 1: Determine the effect of
EAU on organ system identified by system biology approach and by detecting, identifying, and comparing the
relative quantity of these novel targets as potential biomarkers for EAU, and SPECIFIC AIM # 2: To develop
and validate of a risk model for prediction of EAU combining aspects of machine learning and statistical
mechanics. If successful, the results from this project will revolutionize the screening methods for veterans
with excessive alcohol use.

title: Systems Biology Approach to the Management of Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral Bone Disorder
summary:
The derangements of mineral metabolism that accompany chronic kidney disease (CKD) greatly
increase the risk of cardiovascular mortality. Veterans suffer from CKD and the cardiovascular
consequences disproportionately compared to the general population. Amelioration of the
biochemical abnormalities, specifically phosphate (Pi), calcium (Ca), and parathyroid hormone (PTH)
is associated with superior survival in dialysis patients; however, only a minority of patients can
achieve and sustain the levels proposed by Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO)
guidelines. The major barriers are the complexity and individual diversity of CKD-MBD and the
heterogeneity in individual response to therapy. We have developed and validated a systems biology
model encompassing both measurable (serum Ca, Pi, and PTH) as well as non-measurable, clinically
relevant parameters of mineral metabolism such as loss of bone mineral and vascular calcification.
Applying artificial intelligence techniques of reinforcement learning in combination with our model,
we have determined that standard therapeutic approaches targeting Pi, Ca, and PTH may not result in
optimal control of the pathophysiologic processes that result in morbidity and mortality.
These results suggested two hypotheses to be tested in this proposal. Hypothesis 1: Based on
individual biochemical and mineral flux responses to therapy, we can identify phenotypic subsets of
CKD-MBD whose courses of disease are distinct, and which mandate different therapeutic
approaches. Hypothesis 2: Targeting the abnormal fluxes of mineral, out of bone and into the
vascular smooth muscle, will lead to significant refinements in the therapy of CKD-MBD for the
individual by incorporating the degree of bone turnover into the recommendations for achieving
KDIGO guidelines for biochemical parameters.
We will address these hypotheses through the following aims:
Aim 1. Obtain human data on non-routinely measured markers of mineral metabolism and
cardiovascular health within CKD-MBD.
Aim 2. Enhance the Systems Biology Model of CKD-MBD with additional markers of mineral
metabolism.
Aim 3. Develop Systems Biology guided treatment regimen to CKD-MBD based on clinical end points.
Aim 4. Validate treatment regimen for physician’s acceptance using Physician-in-the-Loop approach.
This innovative and highly translational approach will advance the over-arching goal of this project to
improve clinical outcomes for Veterans with CKD-MBD through the application of personalized
therapeutics. The use of large Veteran databases to develop personalized medical therapy for complex
disease, exemplified in this application, is a priority for the Department of Veterans Affairs.

title: Conference: Texas Quantum Winter School 2027
summary:
With support from the CTMC and CSD programs in MPS's Section of Chemistry, Professor Doran Raccah of the University of Texas at Austin, with co-organizer Eric Bittner of the University of Houston, is organizing the second Texas Quantum Winter School (TxQWS). Scheduled for January 3–9, 2027 in Wimberley, Texas, this week-long program is designed for PhD students in theoretical and experimental physical chemistry and chemical physics. The school addresses educational gaps at the interface of quantum information science and chemistry identified by the NSF-UKRI Bilateral Workshop on Quantum Information Science in Chemistry. 

The Winter School provides foundational training at the intersection of quantum information science (QIS) and chemical dynamics, together with a rotating special topic. For 2027, fourteen lectures over five program days pair foundational instruction in quantum information and open-system dynamics with advanced lectures on cavity exciton-polaritons and tensor network methods. Two of the lectures address machine learning for science, and the school will hold regular conversations on best practices for the use of it in research. This format is designed to equip the next generation of scientists with the theoretical and computational skills needed to advance research at the interface of chemistry and quantum information science.

title: CAREER: Nonlinear Factor Analysis for Sensing and Learning
summary:
Factor analysis (FA) tools, e.g., nonnegative matrix factorization (NMF) and independent component analysis (ICA), are the cornerstones of many sensing and learning applications, e.g., document analytics, hyperspectral imaging, brain signal processing, and representation learning. FA tools are designed to discover meaningful latent information from data (e.g., prominent topics in a collection of documents) in an unsupervised manner. However, classic FA models do not consider unknown nonlinear distortions that often happen in data acquisition/generation, and thus frequently fail to produce sensible results in critical scenarios. This project will develop a suite of nonlinear factor analysis (NFA) tools that will transform existing FA paradigms by effectively and provably handling unknown nonlinearities. Results from this project will significantly advance the understanding of fundamental properties and computational aspects of various NFA models, including model identifiability, sample complexity, noise robustness and algorithm convergence---which are largely uncharted research territories. The products will boost the performance of a broad spectrum of sensing and learning tasks in science and engineering where unknown nonlinear distortions often arise, e.g., remote sensing, brain-computer interface, vision/image/text data analytics, bioinformatics, geoscience, biology, and ecology. The integrated education plan of developing visually appealing FA and NFA-based course modules and software will alleviate “math anxiety” in K-12 and college. The precollege outreach programs and undergraduate research plans will effectively foster early interest in mathematics and enhance students’ participation in STEM disciplines. These education activities will lead to a mathematically competitive future workforce for signal and machine intelligence.

This project will develop a unified analytical and computational framework for learning various challenging and realistic NFA models. Specifically, Thrust I will develop a unified functional equation-based framework for provable unsupervised nonlinear model identification under various NFA settings. Thrust II will make important advances towards understanding NFA under realistic conditions (e.g., finite sample and noisy cases), and will offer effective NFA optimization algorithms with performance guarantees. Thrust III will carefully evaluate the proposed approaches over timely and important sensing and learning tasks including hyperspectral imaging, biosensor signal processing, and unsupervised machine learning. These thrusts will produce fundamental results in both theory and algorithms addressing critical challenges in NFA. The new functional equation-based analytical framework offers a theoretical underpinning for various NFA model identification problems that are beyond the reach of existing tools. The new NFA performance characterization tools under realistic settings (e.g., finite data) will be a substantial leap forward from existing works that all use overly ideal assumptions (e.g., unlimited data). The computational framework through an integration of statistical analysis, neural network learning, and nonlinear programming will offer provable and flexible algorithms for NFA problems, which all currently lack guaranteed solutions.

title: Collaborative Research: Unregistered Spectral Image Fusion in Remote Sensing: Foundations and Algorithms
summary:
Remotely sensed spectral images, such as hyperspectral images (HSIs) and multispectral images (MSIs), are widely used across science and engineering fields, including agriculture, oceanography, forest monitoring, mineral discovery, and space exploration. These image modalities involve an inherent trade-off between spatial and spectral resolution: HSIs provide fine spectral detail but coarse spatial resolution, whereas MSIs offer the reverse. Spectral image fusion techniques seek to combine the strengths of both by integrating an HSI and MSI of the same region to produce fused images with high-resolution information in both domains, supporting various tasks such as pixel classification, target identification, and change detection. However, many existing fusion methods operate under the assumption that the spectral images are co-registered (i.e., covering the same region and sharing the same coordinates), whereas in practice the data are often spatially misaligned by pixel shifts, rotations, and other distortions (collectively referred to as “unregistered”), typically arising from differences in sensors or imaging platforms. Despite its fundamental practical importance and considerable interest, the fusion of unregistered spectral images still lacks rigorous theoretical underpinnings and reliable algorithms. This project addresses these gaps by developing new analytical and computational methods to establish a solid theoretical and algorithmic foundation for this long-standing and practically significant problem, enabling performance-guaranteed fusion of unregistered spectral data in real-world scenarios. Beyond remote sensing, the outcomes are expected to benefit areas such as cross-platform medical imaging and domain adaptation/transfer in machine learning. The project also offers undergraduate research opportunities, providing students with training in machine learning, optimization, and image/signal processing.

This project develops a unified, unsupervised framework for fusion of unregistered spectral images with provable guarantees, tackling key challenges including spatial misalignment, lack of training data, and nonrigid deformation. Thrust 1 focuses on establishing theoretical foundations by integrating spectral unmixing with adversarial learning through diversified distribution matching in a latent spatial domain, enabling provable spatio-spectral super-resolution under practical, unregistered scenarios. Thrust 2 extends this framework to more complex real-world cases such as those involving unknown and potentially large nonrigid deformations. Thrust 3 develops stable and efficient optimization algorithms for the proposed fusion formulations, tailored to adversarial learning in latent domains and addressing the limitations of standard optimizers. Validation on semi-realistic and real-world datasets is used to assess the robustness and generalizability of the proposed methods. Expected outcomes include new theoretical insights, practical algorithms with convergence guarantees, and reproducible benchmarks to advance unregistered spectral image fusion and its applications in machine learning, signal processing, and scientific imaging.
